ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Protocol-agnostic Biomedical Image Segmentation using Self-Modifying Attention
PROPOSAL: Train an attention-based segmentation model that can dynamically adapt to multiple segmentation protocols using self-modifying attention mechanisms, allowing it to learn from a diverse range of protocols without explicit protocol specification.
CONTROLS: Establish a baseline using a standard 2D U-Net architecture with standard cross-entropy loss, and then compare with several ablated versions of the self-modifying attention mechanism.
COST: 10,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The self-modifying attention model should outperform the baseline U-Net on a diverse set of segmentation protocols, with a notable improvement in segmenting novel protocols, but may struggle to generalize across extremely large numbers of protocols.

Note: While this proposal appears expensive, the self-modifying attention mechanism can potentially be used in combination with transfer learning to adapt to new protocols, making it a more practical approach than training from scratch for each protocol.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Segmentation Protocol Discovery
PROPOSAL: Use multi-task learning to train a segmentation model to perform both standard segmentation tasks and a novel protocol discovery task, where the model must learn to predict a set of ambiguous labels that correspond to different plausible protocols on a given image.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline model that only performs the standard segmentation task, and an ablated version of the multi-task model that removes the protocol discovery head.
COST: 5,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The multi-task model should improve segmentation accuracy by learning richer feature representations, and the protocol discovery task should provide a useful byproduct of training that can be used to identify the best segmentation protocol for a given image.

Note: By incorporating the protocol discovery task, we hope to encourage the model to learn a more general and robust representation of the image that can be used across multiple protocols. This can potentially lead to better segmentation performance and a better understanding of the underlying image structures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Protocol-Agnostic Segmentation using a Mixture of Experts
PROPOSAL: Train a mixture of experts (MoE) model to segment images under different protocols, where each expert is responsible for a specific protocol and the MoE architecture dynamically selects the most relevant expert for a given image and protocol.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline model that uses a single neural network for all protocols, and an ablated version of the MoE model that removes one or more experts.
COST: 8,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The MoE model should improve segmentation accuracy by selectively using the most relevant protocol-specific expert for each image, but may require careful tuning of the expert selection mechanism to avoid overfitting to specific protocols.

Note: By using a MoE architecture, we can potentially leverage the strengths of multiple protocols and adapt to new protocols by adding or removing experts as needed. This can provide a flexible and efficient solution for protocol-agnostic segmentation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Self-Supervised Learning for Protocol-Agnostic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: Train a segmentation model using self-supervised learning objectives that encourage the model to produce a diverse set of segmentation masks for the same image, promoting the learning of robust and flexible representations that can adapt to different protocols.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline model that uses traditional supervised learning objectives, and ablated versions of the self-supervised learning objectives that remove or modify specific components.
COST: 6,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The self-supervised learning model should improve segmentation accuracy by promoting the learning of robust and flexible representations, but may require careful tuning of the self-supervised learning objectives to avoid overfitting to specific protocols.

Note: By using self-supervised learning objectives, we can encourage the model to learn representations that are robust to variations in image appearance and protocols, which can potentially lead to better segmentation performance and adaptability to new protocols.

TITLE: REVISED Protocol-Agnostic Segmentation using a Mixture of Experts (3)
PROPOSAL: Instead of training a MoE model with a fixed number of experts, use a multi-pooling architecture where each pool is responsible for a subset of protocols, and the outputs from each pool are dynamically weighted to produce the final segmentation mask. This allows the model to adapt to the specific protocols present in a given image.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original MoE model, and an ablated version of the multi-pooling architecture that removes one or more pools.
COST: 7,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised multi-pooling model should improve segmentation accuracy by adaptively weighting the outputs from different pools to match the specific protocols present in a given image, and provide better performance on images with a mixture of protocols.

This revised model aims to address the limitations of the original MoE model by providing a more flexible and adaptive architecture that can handle the presence of multiple protocols in a given image.

PROPOSAL: Modify the self-modifying attention mechanism to use a hierarchical attention structure, where the attention weights are learned at multiple scales, and the attention is dynamically adjusted based on the output from previous scales. This allows the model to adapt to different protocols at different scales.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original self-modifying attention model, and an ablated version of the hierarchical attention structure that removes one or more scales.
COST: 8,000 GPU-hours

TITLE: Efficient Segmentation Protocol Discovery using Submodular Function Maximization
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to efficiently discover segmentation protocols by using submodular function maximization, which can provide an optimal subset of protocols that are relevant for a given image, while avoiding the need to explore the entire protocol space.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline method that uses random sampling to select protocols, and evaluate the performance of submodular function maximization on a set of diverse images.

PROPOSAL: Develop an active learning framework to select the most informative images for human annotation, with the goal of assessing the consistency and accuracy of the discovered protocols. This will enable the identification of protocol inconsistencies and the refinement of the segmentation protocols.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline method that uses random sampling to select images, and evaluate the performance of the active learning framework on a set of diverse images.
COST: 5,000 GPU-hours

PROPOSAL: Develop a set of evaluation metrics that can assess the performance of protocol-agnostic segmentation models across different protocols and images, enabling a fair comparison of their performance.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing evaluation metrics that are specifically designed for single-task segmentation protocols, and evaluate the performance of the proposed metrics on a set of diverse images and protocols.
COST: 3,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed evaluation metrics should provide a comprehensive and fair assessment of the performance of protocol-agnostic segmentation models, helping to identify their strengths and weaknesses and enabling further research in this area.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Universal Protocol-Agnostic Biomedical Image Segmentation
PROPOSAL: Train a self-supervised contrastive learning model (SimCLR) on a large collection of real-world biomedical images with diverse protocols and segmentations, without any manually annotated labels. The model will learn to capture invariant features across protocols and images, allowing it to generate segmentation maps for unseen images and protocols.
CONTROLS: Baseline: random label assignment; Ablation: no contrastive learning, only supervised learning; Control: train on images with limited protocols (e.g., only brain MRI)
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The model will produce diverse and coherent segmentation maps across images, but may struggle with ambiguous or novel protocols, potentially resulting in fragmented or missing structures.

Note: This proposal leverages the use of contrastive learning to extract universal features that are invariant to the segmentation protocol, allowing it to generate plausible segmentations for unseen images and protocols.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Diverse Segmentation Protocol Inference
PROPOSAL: Use a differentiable perturbation-based method to generate a wide range of plausible segmentation protocols for a given image, by iteratively perturbing the initial segmentation and computing the agreement between the perturbed segmentation and the original image features. The method will produce a set of diverse segmentation protocols that can be used as inputs to the universal segmenation model from Proposal 1.
CONTROLS: Control: input perturbations are deterministic and limited in range; Ablation: do not use perturbation-based method, instead use k-means clustering to group pixels by similarity
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method will effectively generate a diverse set of segmentation protocols, but may struggle with highly ambiguous or irregularly shaped structures, potentially resulting in excessive fragmentation.

Note: This proposal uses differentiable perturbation to generate diverse segmentation protocols in a way that complements the universal segmentation model in Proposal 1, which extracts invariant features but may struggle with ambiguity and variability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Conservation of Features across Protocols
PROPOSAL: Theoretically analyze the relationship between the features learned by the universal segmentation model and the features of the input image when different segmentation protocols are applied. Derive a mathematical framework that establishes the conservation of features across protocols, and provide bounds on the difference between the features learned by the model and the true features of the image under different protocols.
CONTROLS: None
COST: 100 GPU-hours (analytical computations)
PREDICTION: This theoretical analysis will provide insights into the behavior of the universal segmentation model under different protocols, and will demonstrate that the model can learn features that are conserved across protocols. However, it may not provide direct bounds or guarantees for the performance of the model on real-world biomedical image segmentation tasks.

Note: This proposal provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the relationship between the universal segmentation model and the features of the input image under different segmentation protocols, complementing the empirical analysis in Proposal 1 and Proposal 2.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Improved Universal Protocol-Agnostic Biomedical Image Segmentation
PROPOSAL: Revise the universal segmentation model from Proposal 1 to incorporate additional inductive biases and regularizations that promote the conservation of features across protocols, as formally established in Proposal 3. Specifically, modify the contrastive loss function to include a term that encourages the model to learn features that are robust to perturbations in the segmentation protocol.
CONTROLS: Baseline: original SimCLR model; Ablation: remove additional regularizations, but keep inductive biases; Control: train on images with limited protocols
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised model should produce more consistent and diversified segmentation protocols across images, while retaining the invariance to segmentation protocols. However, it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to optimize the trade-off between invariance and robustness to perturbations.

Note: This revised proposal combines the insights from Proposal 1, Proposal 2, and Proposal 3 to create a more robust and flexible universal segmentation model that can better capture the conservation of features across protocols.

PROPOSAL: 1 REVISED
PROPOSAL: Modify the universal segmentation model to incorporate an hierarchical structure, where the highest level learns to identify broad anatomical classes (e.g., brain, heart, lung), and lower levels learn to identify finer-grained structures within each class. This hierarchical structure encourages the model to learn invariant features across different protocols, and can facilitate the generation of diverse segmentation protocols at each level.
CONTROLS: Baseline: original SimCLR model; Ablation: remove hierarchical structure, but keep original model architecture; Control: train on images with limited protocols

However, it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to optimize the trade-off between invariance and specificity to anatomical classes.

Note: This revised proposal combines the insights from Proposal 1, Proposal 2, and Proposal 3 to create a more robust and flexible universal segmentation model that can better capture the hierarchical relationship between anatomical structures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Protocol Inference using Human-Annotated Landmarks
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the quality of the segmentation protocols inferred by the diverse segmentation protocol inference method (Proposal 2) using human-annotated landmarks, such as points of interest or regions of interest, that are known to be consistent across different segmentation protocols. Measure the degree of overlap between the inferred protocols and the human-annotated landmarks to assess the accuracy and robustness of the protocol inference method.
CONTROLS: Baseline: evaluate using random labels; Ablation: evaluate using intermediate quality landmark annotations
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This evaluation protocol will provide a more objective and quantitative assessment of the protocol inference method, and will help to identify potential weak points and limitations of the approach. However, it may require careful annotation of landmark points and regions to achieve high accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-Domain Generalization of Protocol-Agnostic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the cross-domain generalizability of the universal protocol-agnostic segmentation model (Proposal 1) and the diverse segmentation protocol inference method (Proposal 2) on a set of images from a clinically relevant but previously unseen domain (e.g., cardiac MRI segmentation using abdominal CT images). Measure the degree of overlap and similarity between the predicted segmentation protocols and the ground truth, as annotated by experts in the target domain.
CONTROLS: Baseline: evaluate on images from similar domain; Ablation: remove cross-dataset selection, use online training with a small set of images from target domain
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This cross-domain evaluation will assess the ability of the protocol-agnostic segmentation approach to generalize across different domains and imaging modalities, and will help to identify potential transfer learning bottlenecks and solutions. However, it may require careful adaptation of the model to the target domain and development of robust evaluation metrics.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Protocol-Agnostic Segmentation for Multi-Organ Segmentation
PROPOSAL: Extend the universal protocol-agnostic segmentation model (Proposal 1) to support multi-organ segmentation by incorporating a hierarchical structure, where each level focuses on the segmentation of a specific organ or anatomical region. This hierarchical approach can help to capture the complex relationships between different organs and improve the overall accuracy of multi-organ segmentation.
CONTROLS: Baseline: use random forest-based approach for multi-organ segmentation; Ablation: remove hierarchical structure, use single-level model for multi-organ segmentation
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This hierarchical protocol-agnostic segmentation approach should improve the overall accuracy and robustness of multi-organ segmentation, particularly in challenging cases involving complex anatomical relationships. However, it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to optimize the trade-off between model complexity and performance.

PROPOSAL: Develop an user-guided refinement module that enables clinicians or researchers to iteratively refine the segmentation protocols and segmentations produced by the protocol-agnostic segmentation approach. This module can incorporate user-provided feedback, such as manual corrections or annotations, to adapt the model and improve its performance on specific clinical tasks or image types.

However, it may require careful design and implementation to ensure that the module is easy to use and effectively incorporates user feedback.

title: protocol-agnostic boundary extraction for consistent segmentation

The goal is to identify common markers or features that can be used to define consistent boundaries across different segmentation protocols.
